title: Neural Networks in Trading: A Spiking Architecture for Spatio-Temporal Market Analysis (Conclusion)
text:
Introduction
The market has always followed its own rules, moving rapidly and unevenly, with constant shifts in pace and sentiment. Every candle on the chart, every spike in the tick stream — each is a small event in a vast mechanism that never stops. What new ideas, one might ask, could possibly be offered in a field where dozens of analytical approaches have already been tried? A field where slow linear models have long since given way to deep neural networks, and modern transformers confidently uncover patterns in multidimensional processes? But financial time series, like the nature of human behavior, continue to stubbornly resist being fully structured. They remain as unpredictable as ever, filled with noise, broken dependencies, and asynchronous dynamics that challenge even the most powerful algorithms.
It is precisely against this backdrop that the need arises, time and again, for models capable of working not just with data, but with
a stream of events
. Not with smoothed candlesticks, but with real-time changes, instantaneous fluctuations, and specific market reactions. Traditional models — even those based on recurrent neural networks or transformers — often fail to capture an important part of market dynamics because they are forced to fit those dynamics into fixed time intervals. The financial environment is much closer to being event-driven; it breathes unevenly — speeding up and slowing down, breaking out of familiar time intervals.
In this sense, spiking architectures have proven to be conceptually closer to the nature of markets than one might have initially assumed. They react to events, generate spikes, and rely on temporal differences, shaping computation into a form that is surprisingly in tune with market chaos. A spiking model does not sample the data once per second. It reacts when there is a reason to react. It does not interpolate empty gaps but skips them, conserving resources and focusing on what really matters.
It was this idea that led us to explore
SDformerFlow
— an architecture originally designed to process event streams from cameras, yet remarkably close in spirit to the task of analyzing tick data. The framework's authors proposed an elegant synthesis of spiking neurons and attention mechanisms, enhancing both approaches. Attention has become more compact and energy-efficient, and the spiking dynamics have become more structured and predictable. The
SDformerFlow
architecture does not just transform a stream of events into meaningful representations — it does so efficiently, consistently, and with a clear internal structure. It is precisely this combination of properties that makes it so appealing for financial applications.
Looking back at the model's key elements, the central role belongs to the
SpatioTemporal Swin SpikeFormer Encoder
(
STSF
) — the heart of the system — which combines convolutional data preprocessing with windowed attention mechanisms and, layer by layer, builds a representation of the structure of the information being analyzed. In the original paper, this module was responsible for extracting the spatiotemporal structure of the optical flow. Small blocks of events were grouped into windows. The windows were shifted so as to cover the entire scene. And then, based on these, a generalized description of the dynamics was developed.
When we apply this approach to trading, we maintain the same general principle. Small segments of a time series — local events, spikes in activity, trend accelerations, and shifts in volatility — play the same role as patches of pixels in an event map in video processing tasks. Financial dynamics are broken down into overlapping windows that allow the model to view the movement from different angles, without overlooking either local or global structures.
This is where one of
SDformerFlow
's key advantages — its adaptability — comes into play. Unlike a classical transformer, where attention is directed to all positions at once — resulting in enormous computational costs — the window mechanism allows for a detailed analysis of local dependencies without overloading the system. At the same time, these shifted windows allow the model to periodically
shake up
its perception and see the big picture. In markets where local patterns often dominate over global structures, this hybrid approach proves particularly valuable.
The spiking component of the architecture completes the picture. It allows the model to respond not to absolute values, but to changes. This aligns perfectly with the nature of tick data. A spiking neuron is activated only when a significant change occurs. During periods of inactivity, it remains silent, creating no unnecessary computational load. This approach simultaneously reduces computational costs and improves resistance to noise — after all, noise is the main problem with financial time series.
The author's visualization of the
SDformerFlow
framework is shown below.
When we began porting
SDformerFlow
to
MQL5
, it became clear that the model's structure naturally lent itself to computational optimization. Its window-based mechanisms and clearly event-driven nature make it possible to parallelize computations. And spiking activity is a natural way to reduce the number of operations. That is precisely why, in previous articles, we implemented the basic building blocks — including spiking attention, residual structures, and modular components — needed to assemble a fully functional encoder block. All of this has laid the foundation for our current work, in which we are moving from individual elements to a cohesive architecture.
We will continue to develop the architecture, gradually integrating all the logic of
SDformerFlow
into a single, functional framework capable of analyzing the market with the precision of an event-driven model and the efficiency of modern transformers.
U
-block
In the previous article, we completed the development of the
SDSA
block — the central component of the
STSF
encoder, which has become a sort of
intellectual center of gravity
for our model. It was in this block that we combined window-based attention, spiking dynamics, and a residual structure to create a mechanism capable of capturing the hidden temporal geometry of the event-driven stream. Now that this block has taken its final form, the next logical step is to move on to building the decoder, since without it, the model remains half-
mute
. It is capable of understanding the structure of the input data, but it is not yet able to transform its internal representations into a meaningful output signal.
When we take another look at the original
SDformerFlow
architecture, we notice an interesting detail. The structure of the decoder's components mirrors the architectural design of the
CNeuronSpikeConvBlock
spiking convolutional block that we have already implemented. This similarity is no coincidence, but rather a deliberate design feature of the model. The authors chose not to create a separate, unconventional design for the decoder. Instead, they used a compact, energy-efficient mechanism that works well and incorporates spiking dynamics and convolutional processing.
This works in our favor. We have already covered the entire process, from low-level implementation to optimizing the convolutional block's compute kernels using
MQL5
and
OpenCL
. We have verified that the module can handle the load, responds correctly to events, and produces stable outputs. That means the architectural foundation is ready, and we do not need to build a new block from scratch.
There is a certain beauty to that. The architecture remains seamless, with no artificial breaks between the encoder and the decoder. All the key elements speak the
same language
—
the language of event-driven convolutions
, spiking activation, and consistent scales. This not only simplifies implementation but also improves the model's stability. Blocks built on the same principles interact with one another in a predictable way, and internal representations easily make the transition from encoding to reconstruction.
The next step in our work is to construct a fully-fledged
U
-shaped architecture that integrates the encoder and decoder into a single multilayer mechanism. In the author's interpretation of
SDformerFlow
, this part of the model looks fairly traditional. The encoder consists of several layers of
SDSA
blocks connected by
SPM
modules (
Spiking Patch Merge
). The data stream then passes sequentially through a cascade of spiking convolutional blocks that make up the decoder. Direct horizontal connections are established between them so that each level of the decoder can receive supplementary information. Thus, the input to each layer of the decoder consists of a concatenated tensor containing the outputs of the previous decoding block and the corresponding layer of the encoder. This approach has long proven its effectiveness in tasks where it is important to combine global coverage with local sensitivity, allowing models to extract structure and reconstruct it at various scales.
However, in our work, we decided to take a slightly different approach. Engineering practice suggests that breaking down the architecture into too many separate objects makes it difficult to implement and maintain the model. This is especially true when dealing with deep structures with multiple levels of nesting, where each layer depends on its neighbor and produces a representation at its own scale. Therefore, instead of implementing the encoder and decoder in separate branches and connecting them manually, we opted for a more compact and elegant solution — building a nested architecture, similar to a matryoshka doll. In this structure, each level contains two components: an encoder and a decoder, connected by a
neck
.
This approach makes it possible to represent the model as a series of self-similar modules, each of which reflects the principles of a
U
-shaped structure, but on a smaller scale. The top level serves as a global framework, and within it lies the next level — exactly the same, but more compact. This continues until,
at the deepest level of nesting
, we reach the
MS-ResBlock
— the final element that serves as the core of our structure and completes the architectural sequence. This solution offers us several advantages at once.
First, this gives us natural symmetry: the encoder and decoder are structured symmetrically at each level and share the context provided by the
neck
. Second, this approach significantly simplifies the management of internal tensors. Data is passed strictly according to the nesting logic, reducing the likelihood of errors and cross-mismatches. Third, in terms of implementation, this proves to be much more convenient — each module becomes not just a block, but an independent structural unit that is easy to manage. And one that is easy to expand, replace, or modify.
But the most important advantage lies in the consistency of the computational flow. In a classic
U
-shaped architecture, data flow constantly switches between different branches, requiring careful management of all connections. In our nested approach, this complexity disappears. Transitions occur within the block's unified space, which makes the architecture more
cohesive
and
stable
. In fact, we obtain a unique variant of a
U
-shaped network, where each level is an independent node containing all the necessary components — an
SDSA
encoder, a spiking convolutional decoder, and a
neck
connecting them, represented by the nested
U
-structure at the next level.
The final level, where an
MS-ResBlock
replaces a further nested structure, will handle the full depth of the computational logic and serve as the center of the final transformation. This block is well-suited to serve as the deepest node. It is stable and compact, has high throughput, and can carefully aggregate signals from all upper levels, laying the foundation for the decoder's return path. Thus, our
recursive architecture
preserves the spirit of the original
SDformerFlow
while adapting to the realities of event-driven markets and the characteristics of
MQL5
— it is compact, hierarchical, and features a high degree of structural repetition.
To implement the nested
U
-shaped architecture, we needed a new structural unit capable of integrating multiple levels of computation and ensuring end-to-end interaction between the block's encoder, decoder, and
neck
. These requirements led us to create a separate object,
CNeuronSDformerUBlock
— the central element that will serve as a building block for our nesting-doll structure. This object encapsulates the logic for bidirectional data flow, data merging, processing, and subsequent reconstruction.

Conceptually, this object builds on the spiking convolutional modules we have already implemented, so inheriting from
CNeuronSpikeConvBlock
is not only natural but also extremely useful. This helps maintain consistency in the computational interface, reuse proven mechanisms, and avoid code duplication. However, the new class significantly extends the functionality of the base block, transforming it from a simple processing module into a full-fledged component of the
U
-shaped architecture.
The object's structure reflects its conceptual role. Three key elements coexist within it. The first is the encoder block,
cEncoder
, which transforms data along the descending path and extracts structural features at the current nesting level. The second is the variable
cNeck
, which represents the
neck
— that is, a nested
U
-block at the next level. It is precisely this mechanism that creates the hierarchical structure of the architecture. Each block contains another, more compact block, until the structure terminates in an
MS-ResBlock
at the lowest nesting level. The third element is the
cConcat
module, which correctly concatenates the tensors from the encoder and the previous level's decoder, with the latter received from the
neck
. We implement the decoder's functionality using the inherited methods of the parent class.
The initialization method acts as a kind of architect for the entire
U
-shaped structure. This is where the abstract scheme — specifying the number of nesting levels, the number of
SDSA
-blocks at each level, and the window and attention-head parameters — becomes an actual set of interacting objects.

Once all elements have been successfully initialized, the structure is considered fully constructed. Each component knows its place, the parameters are consistent, and the connections have been established. Recursive nesting transforms logical abstraction into a hierarchical computational mechanism capable of folding and unfolding signals in complex ways.
At the same time, the forward pass algorithm looks surprisingly clean and well-coordinated, just like a well-rehearsed scene. Every participant knows exactly when to go on stage. Despite the nested nature of the
U
-blocks, the code remains compact and easy to read. And the logic of the computational flow is sequential and intuitive.
bool
CNeuronSDformerUBlock::feedForward(CNeuronBaseOCL *NeuronOCL)
  {
   CNeuronBaseOCL *prev = NeuronOCL;
   CNeuronBaseOCL *curr =
NULL
;
for
(
int
i =
0
; i < cEncoder.Total(); i++)
     {
      curr = cEncoder[i];
if
(!curr ||
         !curr.FeedForward(prev))
return
false
;
      prev = curr;
     }
The forward pass begins with encoder traversal. A chain of
SDSA
blocks and a final
SPM
is formed to process the input data sequentially. Each object receives the output of the previous one as input, gradually condensing the representation and passing it further down the
U
-structure. This part functions as a descending branch — the signal gradually loses redundant spatial detail, transforming into a more concentrated and informative representation.
Next comes the
neck element
, which becomes a key turning point in the computational path. Whether it is the final
MS-Resblock
or a nested
U
-block, the neck object receives the already somewhat compressed features and continues to transform them. At this stage, the data reaches the lowest point of the nested structure, after which an upward movement begins.
if
(!cNeck ||
      !cNeck.FeedForward(prev))
return
false
;
Next, the outputs from the neck and the upper branch of the encoder are concatenated. This step effectively restores the
U
-shaped nature of the structure. The model combines deep features obtained after successive compressions with their
shallower
counterparts, preserving both generalized information and important details. Concatenation forms an extended tensor that serves as the starting point for the decoder and is implemented strictly in accordance with the window sizes and the number of channels, which ensures that the data is assembled correctly.
if
(!Concat(prev.getOutput(), cNeck.getOutput(), cConcat.getOutput(), GetWindow() /
2
,

2
, GetUnits()))

false

U

if
(!CNeuronSpikeConvBlock::feedForward(cConcat.AsObject()))
return
false
;

return
true

The result is an elegant and well-balanced algorithm in which each part of the
U

And now a natural question arises: How does this complex, multilayered structure learn? How does an error propagate through nested levels without getting lost or compromising the stability of the entire architecture? The answer to these questions lies in the gradient calculation mechanism implemented in the
calcInputGradients
method.
Everything here is neatly arranged — as if it were the epilogue to a well-directed play, where every line is delivered at just the right moment and in just the right order. The method acts as the conductor of the backward pass. It carefully retraces the forward pass, distributes errors across the nested levels, and sends the signal back to where it is needed to update the weights.

if
(!NeuronOCL || !cNeck)
return

(!CNeuronSpikeConvBlock::calcInputGradients(cConcat.AsObject()))
return
false

First comes a simple but vital check that the input context and neck node objects exist — without them, there is no point in continuing.
Next, the method of the same name in the parent class is called, which will propagate the error gradients through our decoder module down to the concatenated tensor of the neck and encoder outputs.
Next comes careful
deconcatenation
—
DeConcat
splits the overall gradient into two components: one that goes back to the
neck

encoder

if
(!DeConcat(cConcat.getPrevOutput(), cNeck.getGradient(), cConcat.getGradient(),

2
, GetWindow() /
2
, GetUnits()))
return
false
;
   Deactivation(cNeck)

This is the very moment when the model recalls exactly which inputs it responded to and adjusts the weights based on the sensitivity of the activations.
The backward pass through the encoder begins with the
SPM
block. For this block, hidden gradients with respect to the neck are computed first, followed by backward deactivation and summation with the gradient received from the decoder.

1

i = cEncoder.Total() -
2

0

This call completes the backward pass within the
U
-block and allows higher-level structures to continue propagating errors along the training chain. As a result, the method follows a strict order of operations and is robust against structural errors. At the same time, it is flexible — it correctly handles both a terminal
MS-Resblock
and a recursively nested
U
-block in the
neck
. This design minimizes the likelihood of gradient mismatches between levels and preserves readability even with deep nesting — a quality that is particularly valuable when implementing complex spiking architectures.
Thus,
CNeuronSDformerUBlock
serves as a sort of central hub for the entire structure. The object integrates components into a single whole, elevating the architecture to a new level of abstraction and transforming a complex set of local operations into a coordinated mechanism for building a deep
U
-shaped structure. This object implements the core logic governing end-to-end data flow. The complete code for the class and all of its methods is provided in the attachment.
Top-level Object
At this stage, we have essentially reached the logical conclusion of the implementation. There is one final step left — building a top-level object that will act as a sort of conductor for the entire model. This object defines the overall data flow: from the event sequences being analyzed, through a sequence of nested
U
-blocks, to the generation of the final result.
This object does more than simply combine previously created components. It ensures that their interactions are coordinated. It ensures the correct sequence of forward and backward passes. It provides a single point of control for training parameters. As a result, all layers of the model function as a single entity: they exchange information synchronously, combine multiscale features, and maintain computational stability.
In our implementation, the
CNeuronSDformerFlow
object serves as the crowning element of the entire
SDformerFlow
architecture — the top-level component that integrates the solutions developed so far and defines the model's unified operational logic. If
CNeuronSDformerUBlock
can be thought of as
a building block
or
a nesting doll
, then
CNeuronSDformerFlow
is the framework that holds the entire structure together and keeps it in sync.
Inheriting from
CNeuronSDformerUBlock
gives the object all the benefits of a nested
U
-shaped structure. Building on this,
CNeuronSDformerFlow
adds another layer of control and coordination: the
cFlow
container aggregates all incoming data streams, forming a single channel for processing them and passing them down the hierarchy. This ensures consistency in computations at all levels of nesting and simplifies the management of training and weight updates.

Testing
In this project, we are developing a fully-fledged trading system capable of making decisions and executing trades on its own in the financial market. It operates smoothly, precisely, and confidently, like a trader who knows every twist and turn of the chart.
The model's architecture was largely carried over from previous work without any major changes, which made it possible to retain time-tested signal processing and learning algorithms. The main innovations involved the environment encoder, into which the top-level object
CNeuronSDformerFlow
was integrated. This approach makes it easier to integrate the framework into the model, preserves modularity, and simplifies maintenance. The complete architecture description code is available in the attachment.
Training the model on historical data for the first time is like a novice trader's practice session. Think of
EURUSD
from
January 2024
to
June 2025
as a huge training ground. The model is like a young trader, closely scrutinizing every candlestick, analyzing volume, and looking for patterns between indicators and market reactions.
SDformerFlow
is both a microscope, allowing you to see the minutest movements of each candlestick, and a telescope, revealing global market trends. It generates an informative state for
the Actor
and
the Critic
, combines multiscale features, and learns alongside the model. With each new candlestick, the model learns to predict market movements and assess risks, gradually transforming from a timid learner into a confident practitioner capable of making independent decisions.
The real test comes during the online training phase in the
MetaTrader
5 Strategy Tester. Here, there is no luxury of working calmly with historical data. Each candlestick is like a blow from the real market. The model responds quickly and accurately, analyzes noise fluctuations, adapts to sudden spikes, and adjusts its behavior during periods of low liquidity.
SDformerFlow
combines multiscale features, synchronizes the operation of all blocks, and learns alongside the model.
The final exam is a test on data from
July
through
September
2025
. There are no hints here, no historical data to draw on. Only the market and the model's own decisions. Every market move tests the model's preparedness: how well it has mastered the principles of analysis and learned to combine multiscale features and anticipate market reactions. The test results presented below demonstrate how
SDformerFlow
transforms a complex architecture into a cohesive, adaptive, and efficient trading system capable of performing almost like an experienced trader.
During testing, the model showed a capital increase from

to
133.36 USD
— a steady gain of

. The balance and equity show steady growth with controlled drawdowns and no sharp declines. The maximum drawdown was

The strategy demonstrated moderate profitability with a reasonable level of risk: a profit factor of

, an average winning trade of

. Of the 86 trades, 47 were

(
54.65%
); long positions were profitable
53.52%
of the time, and short positions

of the time. The longest winning streak was

trades, and the longest losing streak was

This confirms the model's stability.
Conclusion
The implemented
SDformerFlow
architecture has become a full-fledged tool for analyzing event-driven financial time series. The model simultaneously captures the slightest market movements and identifies global trends. Each candle and each signal pass through a multilevel
U
-shaped structure, where local and global features are combined, enriching the model's internal state and ensuring forecast accuracy.
The implementation of recursive
U
-blocks and the top-level
CNeuronSDformerFlow
object allowed us to create a single, cohesive organism. The forward and backward passes are coordinated, gradients and weights are updated synchronously, and the entire model is trained harmoniously. This structure ensures the stability of calculations, end-to-end information flow, and the ability to adapt to any market fluctuations, transforming the framework’s theoretical principles into a fully functional trading system.
Test results based on historical data confirm the effectiveness of this approach. Sustained capital growth, controlled drawdowns, and the model’s high adaptability demonstrate the practical value of
SDformerFlow
. The model shows that the combination of multilevel processing, the concatenation of multiscale features, and the synchronization of all blocks makes it a reliable foundation for building modern trading systems.
